name: beyond_weird_benchmark
description: Beyond WEIRD English is a 200-item matched-guise benchmark for evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) comprehension and content-moderation classification across three English varieties: Standard American English (SAE), Standard Indian English (IndEng), and Hinglish (Hindi-English code-mixing). Each item provides three semantically equivalent renditions of the same intent, allowing direct measurement of variety-induced disparities in classification accuracy. The benchmark is fully hand-authored by native Indian-English / Hinglish speakers, contains no scraped or user-generated text, and includes content-moderation labels across six categories (normal, offensive, sexually_suggestive, harassment, violence, self_harm). It is intended as a diagnostic evaluation artifact for measuring the 'Linguistic Gap' (Delta_v) in deployed LLMs.
citeAs: Anonymous authors. Beyond WEIRD English: A Matched-Guise Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Comprehension Across Standard American English, Indian English, and Hinglish. Version 1.0.0 (2026).
rai:dataCollection: All 200 items were hand-authored from scratch by native speakers of Standard Indian English and Hinglish (ages 22-25). For each item, an author selected a moderation category and core semantic intent, wrote the SAE variant, then composed the IndEng and Hinglish variants to preserve meaning while reflecting natural variety-specific phrasing. No web-scraping, no user-generated content, and no LLMs were used at any stage of triplet authoring. Two thematic sub-collections were built: 100 'standard_indianisms' items covering coinages, semantic shifts, syntactic features, and pragmatic markers characteristic of Indian English; and 100 'genz_slang' items covering contemporary Hinglish expressions used by Indian Gen-Z speakers.
rai:dataCollectionType: Hand-authored by domain experts (no scraping; no user-generated text).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each authored item was assigned a single ground-truth moderation category from {normal, offensive, sexually_suggestive, harassment, violence, self_harm}. All 200 items were then validated via survey by 32 adult Indian English speakers (ages 18-30, recruited from the authors' personal networks in Bangalore, Mumbai, Delhi, and Kolkata) who regularly use Hinglish. Each annotator rated each triplet on a 1-5 Likert scale for (i) naturalness of each variety, (ii) cross-variety semantic equivalence, and (iii) agreement with the assigned moderation label. Items with a mean score below 4.0/5.0 (80% of maximum) were rewritten and re-validated until the threshold was met; approximately 40 items (~20%) required at least one revision and 5-6 required a second round of revision.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Web-based opt-in survey form. No paid annotation platform was used. Names and emails were collected only for survey administration and deleted after validation.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Because validation was iterative (items below threshold were rewritten and re-validated until accepted), we report the post-revision acceptance outcome and revision rate (~20% required at least one revision) rather than a static inter-annotator agreement coefficient. Reporting IAA on the post-revision data would be artificially inflated; reporting it on pre-revision data would mischaracterize items that were subsequently improved.
rai:annotatorDemographics: 32 adult volunteers, ages 18-30, residing in major Indian metropolitan areas (Bangalore, Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata). Educational and professional backgrounds spanning undergraduate and graduate education (engineering, commerce, MS/MBA) and professional domains (software, finance). All annotators are fluent IndEng speakers and regular Hinglish users. Annotators were not compensated.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: None. No LLMs or automated tools were used in dataset authoring or annotation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: After validation, items were filtered for (i) PII exclusion (no real names, phone numbers, social handles, addresses, or identifying context), (ii) uniqueness (no duplicate triplets), and (iii) consistent moderation-label assignment. No minimum-length threshold was enforced because many moderation-relevant utterances are short in real deployments.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The benchmark is released as a versioned CSV file under CC BY 4.0. Updates (e.g., expanded coverage to additional World Englishes, additional categories, or annotator demographic broadening) will be released as new versions with semantic-version bumps. The release is hosted at the URL above; the version field tracks the canonical release. The dataset is static (isLiveDataset=false); we do not stream or continuously update items.
rai:dataLimitations: Linguistic coverage is limited to Standard Indian English and Hindi-English code-mixing; it does not cover other South Asian Englishes (Tamil-English, Telugu-English, Bangla-English, etc.) or other World Englishes (Nigerian, Singaporean, etc.).

Annotator pool (32 validators, ages 18-30, all from major Indian metros) skews young, urban, and university-educated. Hinglish usage among older, rural, or non-metro speakers may differ in code-switching frequency, lexical choice, and script conventions.
Category distribution is imbalanced (normal=156, offensive=16, harassment=15, sexually_suggestive=7, self_harm=4, violence=2). Macro-averaged metrics may have high variance for small categories.
Triplet equivalence is a judgment call: pragmatic connotations, register, and cultural resonance may shift across varieties even when propositional content is held constant.

Dataset scale (200 items) is modest relative to large-scale NLP benchmarks; the matched-guise design partially compensates by producing 200 x 3 = 600 evaluation points per model per condition, but small-category subgroup analyses should be interpreted cautiously.
The benchmark is a diagnostic evaluation tool, not a production training corpus. It is not designed for fine-tuning.
rai:dataBiases: Variety bias: Indian English and Hinglish are operationalized as the urban Gen-Z register most familiar to the authors and validators. Older, rural, or regional registers may be under-represented.

Category bias: The moderation taxonomy follows common Western/SAE-trained content-moderation systems (normal, offensive, sexually_suggestive, harassment, violence, self_harm). Indigenous Indian moderation taxonomies (e.g., caste-based slurs, communal speech) are not separately surfaced as top-level categories.

Selection bias in lexical seeds: items were selected to surface variety-induced classification disparities; the benchmark deliberately includes asymmetry probes (e.g., dicky/pant/ragging) and may over-represent items where SAE-IndEng-Hinglish processing diverges relative to a uniform random sample of Indian English usage.
rai:dataUseCases: Measuring per-variety accuracy of LLM content-moderation classifiers for English-input pipelines.
Computing the Linguistic Gap metric Delta_v = f(model, SAE) - f(model, v) for v in {Indian English, Hinglish}.
Stress-testing safety-filter robustness across English varieties (matched-guise probes for over-blocking and under-blocking).
Benchmarking the effect of inference-time interventions (e.g., chain-of-thought, dialect-aware prompting) on dialect robustness.
Auditing deployed LLM systems serving Indian English / Hinglish user populations for variety-induced disparities.
Comparing LLMs across model families on a matched-semantics evaluation, removing content-distribution as a confound.
rai:dataUseCasesOutOfScope: Training a content-moderation classifier (the benchmark is too small and is intended as evaluation, not training).
Generalizing claims to non-evaluated English varieties (other South Asian Englishes, African Englishes, etc.) without re-validation.

Generalizing claims beyond content moderation to arbitrary downstream tasks; the benchmark uses moderation as a diagnostic and may not transfer to generation, dialogue, or long-context tasks without further evidence.
Operational deployment as a real-time moderation oracle. The dataset is a static evaluation set, not a production rule set.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The benchmark contains no personally identifiable information (PII) and no verbatim user-generated text. All examples are hand-authored. No real names, handles, phone numbers, addresses, or identifying context appear in any item. Validator names and email addresses were collected only for survey administration and were deleted after validation; only aggregate statistics are reported.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Positive: provides a public, reproducible measurement instrument for an under-measured axis of LLM disparity (linguistic variety within English) affecting hundreds of millions of Indian English / Hinglish users. Encourages disaggregated reporting of LLM evaluation results across English varieties. Negative / dual-use: the benchmark contains items that probe sensitive moderation categories (e.g., harassment, self-harm). The release adopts a responsible-disclosure posture: aggregate reporting is prioritized over verbatim harmful exemplars, and we explicitly avoid publishing exploit-ready prompt templates. Misframing risk: results should not be read as evidence that Indian English or Hinglish are deficient varieties; the documented failures are failures of model training and evaluation, not of speakers.
rai:dataSensitiveContent: The benchmark deliberately includes sensitive moderation categories (harassment, violence, self_harm, sexually_suggestive, offensive) so that variety-induced moderation disparities can be measured. Downstream users should treat the dataset as containing sensitive material and provide content warnings to human readers.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenanceContact: Contact details are withheld during anonymous review and will be added to the public release.

distribution.name: beyond_weird_benchmark.csv
distribution.description: Canonical CSV release of the 200-item matched-guise benchmark. One row per item; columns include the three variety renditions (sae_example, indian_english_translation, hinglish_example), the source word/phrase, the human-authored ground-truth meaning gloss, the moderation category label, and the dataset sub-collection (standard_indianisms or genz_slang).

recordSet.name: items
recordSet.description: One record per benchmark item. Each item provides three semantically-equivalent renditions of the same intent (Hinglish, Indian English, Standard American English), the source word/phrase, the authored meaning gloss, the ground-truth moderation category, and the sub-collection tag.

field.name: id
field.description: Unique integer identifier for the benchmark item (1-200).

field.name: word_or_phrase
field.description: The seed Indian English word or phrase that the item is built around (e.g., 'passed out', 'dicky', 'prepone').

field.name: hinglish_example
field.description: The Hinglish (Hindi-English code-mixed) rendition of the item's intent.

field.name: indian_english_translation
field.description: The Standard Indian English rendition of the item's intent.

field.name: sae_example
field.description: The Standard American English rendition of the item's intent.

field.name: indian_meaning
field.description: Human-authored prose gloss of the item's intended meaning, written in Indian English.

field.name: category
field.description: Ground-truth moderation category. One of: normal, offensive, sexually_suggestive, harassment, violence, self_harm.

field.name: dataset_type
field.description: Sub-collection tag. One of: 'standard_indianisms' (100 items covering Indian English coinages, semantic shifts, syntactic / pragmatic features) or 'genz_slang' (100 items covering contemporary Indian Gen-Z Hinglish expressions).
